title: CUET Physics Test 1
subject: Physics (Code: 322)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Physics - 322.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Physics papers 2024, 2025 and 2026, analysed for format and level (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Physics, Class XII, Parts I and II (rationalised edition)
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
Calculators are not allowed; numbers are chosen so the working can be done by hand.

questions.sub_topic: Ratio of the radii of aluminium-27 and tellurium-125 nuclei
questions.question: The ratio of the nuclear radii of \(^{27}_{13}\text{Al}\) and \(^{125}_{52}\text{Te}\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(3 : 5\)
Given: \(A_1 = 27\), \(A_2 = 125\)
Formula: \(R = R_0A^{1/3}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \left(\dfrac{27}{125}\right)^{1/3}\)
Step 2: \(= \dfrac{3}{5}\)
Common mistake: \(13 : 52\) (D) uses atomic numbers. \(27 : 125\) (A) forgets the cube root.
Key point: Nuclear volume is proportional to \(A\), so all nuclei have about the same density.

questions.sub_topic: Nuclear terms
questions.question:
Match each term in List-I with its description in List-II.

List-I
(A) Isotopes
(B) Isobars
(C) Isotones
(D) Nuclear force

List-II
(I) Same atomic number, different mass numbers
(II) Short-range and nearly independent of charge
(III) Same mass number, different atomic numbers
(IV) Same number of neutrons
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Step 1: Isotopes (e.g. \(^{1}\text{H}\), \(^{2}\text{H}\)): same \(Z\) (I)
Step 2: Isobars (e.g. \(^{3}\text{H}\), \(^{3}\text{He}\)): same \(A\) (III)
Step 3: Isotones (e.g. \(^{3}\text{H}\), \(^{4}\text{He}\)): same \(N = A - Z\) (IV)
Step 4: The nuclear force acts only over a few femtometres and is the same for p–p, n–n and n–p (II)
Common mistake: Swapping (A) and (B); remember isoto**p**es share **p**rotons.
Key point: \(A = Z + N\).

questions.sub_topic: Resistance of a 100 W, 220 V bulb
questions.question: The resistance of a bulb rated 100 W, 220 V is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(484\ \Omega\)
Given: \(P = 100\) W, \(V = 220\) V
Formula: \(R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}\)
Step 1: \(R = \dfrac{48400}{100} = 484\ \Omega\)
Common mistake: \(2.2\ \Omega\) (A) divides \(V\) by \(P\).
Key point: The rating gives the resistance at the rated voltage.

questions.sub_topic: Focal length of a convex and a concave lens in contact
questions.question: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm is placed in contact with a concave lens of focal length 15 cm. The combination has a focal length of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(+30\) cm
Given: \(f_1 = +10\) cm, \(f_2 = -15\) cm
Formula: \(\dfrac{1}{F} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{F} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{1}{30}\)
Step 2: \(F = +30\) cm (converging)
Common mistake: \(+6\) cm (C) adds the powers as if both lenses were convex.
Key point: The stronger lens decides whether the combination converges.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Behaviour of magnetic materials — which claims fail
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Diamagnetic substances have a small negative susceptibility.
(B) The susceptibility of a paramagnetic substance decreases as its temperature rises.
(C) A ferromagnetic substance stays ferromagnetic at every temperature.
(D) A superconductor behaves as a perfect diamagnet.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: above its Curie temperature a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic.
Why not the others: (A) diamagnets are weakly repelled, \(\chi < 0\). (B) Curie's law: \(\chi \propto \dfrac{1}{T}\). (D) superconductors expel the field completely (Meissner effect), \(\chi = -1\). Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Heating destroys the alignment of domains in a ferromagnet.

questions.sub_topic: Four resistance results
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) \(3\ \Omega\) and \(6\ \Omega\) in parallel
(B) \(2\ \Omega\) and \(4\ \Omega\) in series
(C) A \(3\ \Omega\) wire stretched to twice its length
(D) Internal resistance of a 2 V cell whose terminal voltage is 1.6 V across a \(4\ \Omega\) resistor

List-II
(I) \(12\ \Omega\)
(II) \(1\ \Omega\)
(III) \(2\ \Omega\)
(IV) \(6\ \Omega\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{3 \times 6}{3 + 6} = 2\ \Omega\) (III)
Step 2: \(2 + 4 = 6\ \Omega\) (IV)
Step 3: Volume fixed, so length ×2 and area ÷2: \(R \propto \dfrac{l}{A}\) rises 4 times: \(12\ \Omega\) (I)
Step 4: \(I = \dfrac{1.6}{4} = 0.4\) A; \(r = \dfrac{2 - 1.6}{0.4} = 1\ \Omega\) (II)
Common mistake: Giving \(6\ \Omega\) for (C) by doubling only the length; stretching also halves the area.
Key point: A wire stretched \(n\) times has \(n^2\) times the resistance.

questions.sub_topic: Energy of the hydrogen electron in the second orbit
questions.question: In the Bohr model, the energy of the electron in the \(n = 2\) orbit of hydrogen is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(-3.4\) eV
Given: \(n = 2\)
Formula: \(E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}\) eV
Step 1: \(E_2 = -\dfrac{13.6}{4} = -3.4\) eV
Common mistake: \(-6.8\) eV (B) divides by \(n\) instead of \(n^2\). \(-1.51\) eV (C) is \(n = 3\).
Key point: Energy levels crowd together as \(n\) grows.

questions.sub_topic: emf induced by a falling flux through 50 turns
questions.question: The flux through each turn of a 50-turn coil falls from 8 mWb to 2 mWb in 0.1 s. The average induced emf is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3 V
Given: \(N = 50\), \(\Delta\Phi = 6 \times 10^{-3}\) Wb, \(\Delta t = 0.1\) s
Formula: \(|\varepsilon| = N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = 0.06\) Wb s⁻¹
Step 2: \(\varepsilon = 50 \times 0.06 = 3\) V
Common mistake: 0.06 V (A) forgets the number of turns.
Key point: Each turn adds its own emf.

questions.sub_topic: Binding energy per nucleon of helium-4
questions.question: The mass defect of a \(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\) nucleus is 0.0304 u. Its binding energy per nucleon is about (1 u = 931.5 MeV):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 7.07 MeV
Given: \(\Delta m = 0.0304\) u, \(A = 4\)
Formula: \(E_b = \Delta m \times 931.5\) MeV
Step 1: \(E_b = 0.0304 \times 931.5 \approx 28.3\) MeV
Step 2: Per nucleon: \(\dfrac{28.3}{4} \approx 7.07\) MeV
Common mistake: 28.3 MeV (A) is the total binding energy. 14.15 MeV (C) divides by the 2 protons only.
Key point: Divide by the mass number to get the binding energy per nucleon.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Force on a wire at 30° to a field
questions.question: A wire 0.5 m long carrying 2 A lies at \(30^\circ\) to a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T. The force on it is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.2 N
Given: \(I = 2\) A, \(l = 0.5\) m, \(B = 0.4\) T, \(\theta = 30^\circ\)
Formula: \(F = IlB\sin\theta\)
Step 1: \(IlB = 0.4\)
Step 2: \(F = 0.4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.2\) N
Common mistake: 0.35 N (B) uses \(\cos 30^\circ\). 0.4 N (A) takes the wire perpendicular to the field.
Key point: Only the component of the wire perpendicular to \(B\) feels a force.

questions.sub_topic: Total internal reflection, Huygens and diffraction — which claims fail
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In single-slit diffraction, the central maximum gets wider when the slit is made wider.
(B) Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets.
(C) Total internal reflection needs light to go from a denser to a rarer medium.
(D) Sustained interference needs coherent sources.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false: the angular width of the central maximum is \(\dfrac{2\lambda}{a}\), so a wider slit gives a narrower maximum.
Why not the others: (B) is Huygens' principle. (C) the critical angle exists only when \(n_1 > n_2\). (D) a fixed phase difference is needed for a steady pattern. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Diffraction is strongest when the slit is narrow, comparable to the wavelength.

questions.sub_topic: Field inside a charged thin spherical shell
questions.question: A thin spherical shell of radius \(R\) carries charge \(Q\) spread uniformly. The electric field at a point \(\dfrac{R}{2}\) from its centre is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) zero
Why: A Gaussian sphere of radius \(\dfrac{R}{2}\) encloses no charge, so by Gauss's theorem the flux, and by symmetry the field, is zero.
Why not the others: (A) is the field just outside the surface. (B) treats the charge as a point charge at the centre seen from \(\dfrac{R}{2}\). (D) has no basis.
Key point: All the charge of a shell lies outside any Gaussian surface drawn inside it.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Fields of four 1 A arrangements in increasing order
questions.question:
Each arrangement carries a current of 1 A:
(A) the centre of a circular loop of radius 10 cm
(B) a point 10 cm from a long straight wire
(C) inside a long solenoid with 1000 turns per metre
(D) a point 1 cm from a long straight wire
Arrange them in increasing order of the magnetic field.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (A), (D), (C)
Step 1: (B) \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7}}{0.1} = 2 \times 10^{-6}\) T
Step 2: (A) \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}{0.2} \approx 6.3 \times 10^{-6}\) T
Step 3: (D) \(\dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7}}{0.01} = 2 \times 10^{-5}\) T
Step 4: (C) \(\mu_0nI = 4\pi \times 10^{-4} \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-3}\) T
Common mistake: Putting (A) below (B); at the same distance the loop's field is \(\pi\) times the wire's.
Key point: A solenoid concentrates the field of many turns.

questions.sub_topic: What most α-particles passing straight through shows
questions.question: In the Rutherford scattering experiment, most α-particles passed through the gold foil almost undeflected. This shows that:
options: A) most of the atom is empty space
B) electrons move in fixed orbits
C) the nucleus is negatively charged
D) the mass of the atom is spread uniformly
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) most of the atom is empty space
Why: An α-particle is deflected only when it passes close to the tiny, heavy, positive nucleus; most pass far from any nucleus.
Why not the others: (B) came later from Bohr. (C) the large-angle repulsion shows a positive nucleus. (D) is Thomson's model, which this experiment disproved.
Key point: The few large-angle deflections show that the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: de Broglie wavelength of an electron through 100 V
questions.question: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through 100 V is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.123 nm
Given: \(V = 100\) V
Formula: \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} = \dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\) nm
Step 1: \(\sqrt{100} = 10\)
Step 2: \(\lambda = 0.1227 \approx 0.123\) nm
Common mistake: 1.23 nm (A) is the value for 1 V. 0.0123 nm (C) divides by \(V\) instead of \(\sqrt{V}\).
Key point: Electron wavelengths at ordinary voltages are comparable to atomic spacings.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Radius of a proton's circle in a magnetic field
questions.question: A proton (\(m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg) moves at \(2 \times 10^6\) m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a field of 0.5 T. The radius of its circular path is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 4.2 cm
Given: \(m = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg, \(v = 2 \times 10^6\) m s⁻¹, \(q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C, \(B = 0.5\) T
Formula: \(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\)
Step 1: \(mv = 3.34 \times 10^{-21}\); \(qB = 8 \times 10^{-20}\)
Step 2: \(r = \dfrac{3.34 \times 10^{-21}}{8 \times 10^{-20}} \approx 0.042\) m \(= 4.2\) cm
Common mistake: 2.1 cm (A) uses \(r = \dfrac{mv}{2qB}\).
Key point: The magnetic force \(qvB\) supplies the centripetal force \(\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\).

questions.sub_topic: Focal length of an equiconvex lens from the lens maker's formula
questions.question: An equiconvex lens has both radii of curvature 20 cm and refractive index 1.5. Its focal length is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 20 cm
Given: \(R_1 = +20\) cm, \(R_2 = -20\) cm, \(n = 1.5\)
Formula: \(\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{f} = 0.5 \times \dfrac{2}{20} = \dfrac{1}{20}\)
Step 2: \(f = 20\) cm
Common mistake: 40 cm (C) counts only one curved surface, \(\dfrac{1}{f} = 0.5 \times \dfrac{1}{20}\).
Key point: For an equiconvex lens with \(n = 1.5\), \(f = R\).

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Shunt that turns a galvanometer into a 5 A ammeter
questions.question: A galvanometer of resistance \(50\ \Omega\) gives full-scale deflection for 5 mA. The shunt needed to convert it into an ammeter of range 5 A is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(0.05\ \Omega\)
Given: \(G = 50\ \Omega\), \(I_g = 5 \times 10^{-3}\) A, \(I = 5\) A
Formula: \(S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I - I_g}\)
Step 1: \(I_gG = 0.25\) V
Step 2: \(S = \dfrac{0.25}{4.995} \approx 0.05\ \Omega\)
Common mistake: \(49.95\ \Omega\) (D) treats it as a series resistance, which is how a voltmeter is made.
Key point: An ammeter needs a small resistance in parallel; a voltmeter needs a large one in series.

questions.sub_topic: Point of zero force between +4q and +q
questions.question: Charges \(+4q\) and \(+q\) are fixed 3 m apart. A third charge feels no net force when placed on the line joining them at a distance from \(+4q\) of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2 m
Given: let the point be \(x\) from \(+4q\), so \(3 - x\) from \(+q\)
Formula: equal forces: \(\dfrac{4q}{x^2} = \dfrac{q}{(3 - x)^2}\)
Step 1: Take square roots: \(\dfrac{2}{x} = \dfrac{1}{3 - x}\)
Step 2: \(6 - 2x = x \Rightarrow x = 2\) m
Common mistake: 1 m (A) puts the point nearer the larger charge; the null point of two like charges lies nearer the smaller one.
Key point: For like charges the null point is between them, closer to the smaller charge.

questions.sub_topic: Four optics results
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Power of a convex lens of focal length 25 cm
(B) Magnifying power of a telescope with \(f_o = 100\) cm and \(f_e = 5\) cm (normal adjustment)
(C) Fringe width for \(\lambda = 600\) nm, \(D = 1\) m, \(d = 1\) mm
(D) Critical angle for a medium of refractive index 2

List-II
(I) \(30^\circ\)
(II) 20
(III) \(+4\) D
(IV) 0.6 mm
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Step 1: \(P = \dfrac{1}{0.25\ \text{m}} = +4\) D (III)
Step 2: \(m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = 20\) (II)
Step 3: \(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1}{10^{-3}} = 0.6\) mm (IV)
Step 4: \(\sin C = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(C = 30^\circ\) (I)
Common mistake: Writing \(P = \dfrac{1}{25} = 0.04\) D for (A); the focal length must be in metres.
Key point: Power in dioptres needs \(f\) in metres.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Energy of a 620 nm photon in eV
questions.question: The energy of a photon of wavelength 620 nm is about (\(hc = 1240\) eV nm):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2 eV
Given: \(\lambda = 620\) nm
Formula: \(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\)
Step 1: \(E = \dfrac{1240}{620} = 2\) eV
Common mistake: 0.5 eV (C) inverts the ratio, \(\dfrac{\lambda}{hc} = \dfrac{620}{1240}\).
Key point: \(E\,(\text{eV}) = \dfrac{1240}{\lambda\,(\text{nm})}\).

questions.sub_topic: Drift speed in a copper wire
questions.question: A copper wire of cross-section 1 mm² carries 1.5 A. If \(n = 8.5 \times 10^{28}\) m⁻³, the drift speed of the electrons is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1.1 \times 10^{-4}\) m s⁻¹
Given: \(I = 1.5\) A, \(A = 10^{-6}\) m², \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C
Formula: \(v_d = \dfrac{I}{neA}\)
Step 1: \(neA = 8.5 \times 10^{28} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{-6} = 1.36 \times 10^4\)
Step 2: \(v_d = \dfrac{1.5}{1.36 \times 10^4} \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-4}\) m s⁻¹
Common mistake: \(1.1 \times 10^{-2}\) m s⁻¹ (C) uses 1 mm² as \(10^{-4}\) m².
Key point: 1 mm² = \(10^{-6}\) m²; drift speeds are fractions of a millimetre per second.

questions.sub_topic: Displacement current while a capacitor charges
questions.question: While a parallel plate capacitor is being charged, the displacement current between its plates is:
options: A) zero, because no charge crosses the gap between the plates
B) equal to the conduction current in the wires
C) greater than the conduction current in the wires
D) opposite in direction to the current in the wires
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) equal to the conduction current in the wires
Why: The changing electric field between the plates gives \(i_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\), and this equals the conduction current \(\dfrac{dQ}{dt}\), so the total current is continuous.
Why not the others: (A) ignores the changing field. (C) and (D) would break the continuity of current.
Key point: Maxwell added the displacement current so that Ampere's law holds across the gap.

questions.sub_topic: Energy lost when a charged capacitor shares charge
questions.question: A \(4\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor charged to 50 V is disconnected and joined across an uncharged \(6\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor. The energy lost in the process is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3 mJ
Given: \(Q = 4 \times 10^{-6} \times 50 = 2 \times 10^{-4}\) C, shared by \(10\ \mu\text{F}\)
Formula: \(U = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2\); common \(V = \dfrac{Q}{C_1 + C_2}\)
Step 1: \(U_i = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 10^{-6} \times 2500 = 5\) mJ
Step 2: \(V = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-4}}{10^{-5}} = 20\) V; \(U_f = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10^{-5} \times 400 = 2\) mJ
Step 3: Loss \(= 5 - 2 = 3\) mJ
Common mistake: 2 mJ (B) is the final energy, not the loss. 5 mJ (C) is the initial energy.
Key point: Charge is conserved when capacitors share charge; energy is not (it is lost as heat and radiation).

questions.sub_topic: rms value of 311 sin(100πt) volts
questions.question: An a.c. voltage is \(V = 311\sin(100\pi t)\) volts. Its rms value is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 220 V
Given: \(V_0 = 311\) V
Formula: \(V_{rms} = \dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{311}{1.414} \approx 220\) V
Common mistake: 155.5 V (B) halves the peak value instead of dividing by \(\sqrt{2}\).
Key point: Household "220 V" is an rms value; the peak is about 311 V.

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Field formulas for four current arrangements
questions.question:
Match each arrangement in List-I with the magnitude of its magnetic field in List-II.

List-I
(A) Centre of a circular loop of radius \(R\) carrying \(I\)
(B) Distance \(r\) from a long straight wire carrying \(I\)
(C) Inside a long solenoid with \(n\) turns per unit length carrying \(I\)
(D) Axial point at distance \(r\) from a short bar magnet of moment \(m\)

List-II
(I) \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}\)
(II) \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}\)
(III) \(\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3}\)
(IV) \(\mu_0nI\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Step 1: Biot–Savart at the centre of a loop: \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}\) (II)
Step 2: Ampere's law around a wire: \(\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}\) (I)
Step 3: Ampere's law for a solenoid: \(\mu_0nI\) (IV)
Step 4: Axial field of a magnetic dipole: \(\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3}\) (III)
Common mistake: Swapping (A) and (B); the loop has no \(\pi\) in the denominator, the straight wire does.
Key point: A dipole's field falls as \(\dfrac{1}{r^3}\); a long wire's as \(\dfrac{1}{r}\).

questions.sub_topic: Induction and a.c. basics — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of energy.
(B) Inserting a soft iron core into a solenoid increases its self-inductance.
(C) In a purely inductive a.c. circuit, the current lags the voltage by \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
(D) The average power taken by a pure capacitor over a full cycle is maximum.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) an induced current that aided the change would create energy from nothing. (B) \(L \propto \mu_r\). (C) \(V_L\) leads \(I\) by \(90^\circ\).
Why not the others: (D) is false: with a \(90^\circ\) phase difference, \(\cos\phi = 0\), so the average power is zero. Options (C) and (D) include (D); (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: Pure L and pure C take no average power; the current through them is wattless.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Observations of the photoelectric effect — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the photoelectric effect:
(A) Above the threshold frequency, the photocurrent increases with the intensity of light.
(B) The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depends on the frequency, not on the intensity.
(C) The stopping potential increases with the intensity of light.
(D) Emission begins practically at the instant light falls on the surface.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A) more photons per second free more electrons. (B) \(K_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0\) has no intensity term. (D) each photon gives its energy to one electron at once.
Why not the others: (C) is false: the stopping potential measures \(K_{max}\), which does not depend on intensity. Options (B) and (D) include (C); (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: Intensity controls how many electrons; frequency controls how fast.

questions.sub_topic: Magnetic field amplitude from E₀ = 30 V/m
questions.question: The electric field amplitude of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum is 30 V m⁻¹. Its magnetic field amplitude is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1 \times 10^{-7}\) T
Given: \(E_0 = 30\) V m⁻¹, \(c = 3 \times 10^8\) m s⁻¹
Formula: \(B_0 = \dfrac{E_0}{c}\)
Step 1: \(B_0 = \dfrac{30}{3 \times 10^8} = 1 \times 10^{-7}\) T
Common mistake: \(9 \times 10^9\) T (B) multiplies by \(c\).
Key point: In an EM wave, \(E_0 = cB_0\).

questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.sub_topic: Force per metre between two parallel wires
questions.question: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 5 A and 10 A in the same direction. The force per metre between them is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(1 \times 10^{-4}\) N m⁻¹, attractive
Given: \(I_1 = 5\) A, \(I_2 = 10\) A, \(d = 0.1\) m
Formula: \(\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 50}{0.1} = 1 \times 10^{-4}\) N m⁻¹
Step 2: Currents in the same direction attract
Common mistake: (A) gets the size right but the direction wrong; like currents attract, unlike currents repel.
Key point: This force defines the ampere.

questions.sub_topic: Conductors and equipotential surfaces — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Inside a charged conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field is zero.
(B) Electric field lines are perpendicular to an equipotential surface at every point.
(C) The electric potential inside a charged hollow conducting sphere is zero.
(D) No work is done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A) free charges move until the field inside vanishes. (B) a field component along the surface would make the potential change along it. (D) \(W = q\Delta V = 0\) when \(\Delta V = 0\).
Why not the others: (C) is false: the field inside is zero, so the potential inside is constant and equal to its value on the surface, \(\dfrac{kQ}{R}\), not zero. Options (C) and (D) include (C); (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: Zero field means constant potential, not zero potential.

questions.sub_topic: Fourth arm of a balanced Wheatstone bridge
questions.question: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, \(P = 2\ \Omega\), \(Q = 3\ \Omega\) and \(R = 4\ \Omega\). The fourth resistance \(S\) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(6\ \Omega\)
Given: balance condition \(\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}\)
Formula: \(S = \dfrac{QR}{P}\)
Step 1: \(S = \dfrac{3 \times 4}{2} = 6\ \Omega\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{8}{3}\ \Omega\) (A) uses \(S = \dfrac{PR}{Q}\).
Key point: At balance no current flows through the galvanometer, so the ratios of adjacent arms are equal.

questions.sub_topic: Image by a concave mirror for an object at 15 cm
questions.question: An object is 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image is formed:
options: A) 6 cm behind the mirror, erect
B) 30 cm behind the mirror, erect
C) 30 cm in front of the mirror, inverted and magnified
D) 6 cm in front of the mirror, inverted and diminished
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 30 cm in front of the mirror, inverted and magnified
Given: \(u = -15\) cm, \(f = -10\) cm
Formula: \(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{15} = -\dfrac{1}{30}\), so \(v = -30\) cm (in front)
Step 2: \(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -2\): inverted, twice the size
Common mistake: (D) uses \(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u}\), mixing the lens and mirror forms.
Key point: An object between \(F\) and \(C\) gives a real, inverted, magnified image beyond \(C\).

questions.sub_topic: Refractive index of a prism from its minimum deviation
questions.question: A prism of angle \(60^\circ\) gives a minimum deviation of \(30^\circ\). Its refractive index is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\sqrt{2}\)
Given: \(A = 60^\circ\), \(\delta_m = 30^\circ\)
Formula: \(n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2} = 45^\circ\), \(\dfrac{A}{2} = 30^\circ\)
Step 2: \(n = \dfrac{1/\sqrt{2}}{1/2} = \sqrt{2}\)
Common mistake: \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) (D) inverts the ratio, giving \(n < 1\).
Key point: At minimum deviation the ray passes through the prism symmetrically.

questions.sub_topic: Colours in increasing order of deviation by a prism
questions.question:
White light passes through a glass prism. Arrange these colours in increasing order of their deviation:
(A) red
(B) violet
(C) green
(D) yellow
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (D), (C), (B)
Step 1: Glass has a larger refractive index for shorter wavelengths
Step 2: Wavelength order: red > yellow > green > violet
Step 3: So deviation increases: red, yellow, green, violet: (A), (D), (C), (B)
Common mistake: (A) reverses the order, giving red the largest deviation.
Key point: Violet bends most, red least.

questions.sub_topic: Coulomb force between 2 μC and 3 μC at 30 cm
questions.question: The force between point charges of \(2\ \mu\text{C}\) and \(3\ \mu\text{C}\) placed 30 cm apart in air is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(0.6\) N
Given: \(q_1 = 2 \times 10^{-6}\) C, \(q_2 = 3 \times 10^{-6}\) C, \(r = 0.3\) m
Formula: \(F = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2}\)
Step 1: \(kq_1q_2 = 9 \times 10^9 \times 6 \times 10^{-12} = 5.4 \times 10^{-2}\)
Step 2: \(F = \dfrac{5.4 \times 10^{-2}}{0.09} = 0.6\) N
Common mistake: \(0.18\) N (B) divides by \(r\) instead of \(r^2\).
Key point: Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law.

questions.sub_topic: Materials in increasing order of band gap
questions.question:
Arrange these in increasing order of the energy gap between the valence and conduction bands:
(A) germanium
(B) silicon
(C) diamond
(D) copper
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (D), (A), (B), (C)
Step 1: Copper is a metal: the bands overlap, gap 0 (D)
Step 2: Germanium about 0.7 eV (A), silicon about 1.1 eV (B)
Step 3: Diamond about 5.4 eV, an insulator (C)
Common mistake: (B) puts silicon below germanium.
Key point: Conductor < semiconductor < insulator in band gap.

questions.sub_topic: Four kinds of solids by their carriers and gaps
questions.question:
Match each material in List-I with its property in List-II.

List-I
(A) Intrinsic semiconductor
(B) n-type semiconductor
(C) p-type semiconductor
(D) Insulator

List-II
(I) Doped with a trivalent element such as boron
(II) Equal numbers of free electrons and holes
(III) Band gap larger than about 3 eV
(IV) Doped with a pentavalent element such as arsenic
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Step 1: Pure semiconductor: \(n_e = n_h\) (II)
Step 2: A pentavalent donor gives a spare electron (IV)
Step 3: A trivalent acceptor leaves a hole (I)
Step 4: An insulator's gap is too wide for thermal excitation (III)
Common mistake: Swapping (B) and (C); **p**entavalent gives **n**-type, not p-type.
Key point: Donors (group 15) make n-type; acceptors (group 13) make p-type.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.sub_topic: Stopping potential for 400 nm light on a 2.3 eV surface
questions.question: Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.3 eV. The stopping potential is about (\(hc = 1240\) eV nm):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.8 V
Given: \(\lambda = 400\) nm, \(\phi_0 = 2.3\) eV
Formula: \(eV_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi_0\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1240}{400} = 3.1\) eV
Step 2: \(eV_0 = 3.1 - 2.3 = 0.8\) eV, so \(V_0 = 0.8\) V
Common mistake: 3.1 V (A) forgets to subtract the work function. 5.4 V (D) adds it.
Key point: The photon pays the work function first; the rest is kinetic energy.

questions.sub_topic: SI unit of inductance
questions.question: The SI unit of self-inductance is the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) henry
Why: \(L = \dfrac{\Phi}{I}\), so its unit is Wb A⁻¹, named the henry (H).
Why not the others: The tesla measures magnetic field, the weber magnetic flux, and the farad capacitance.
Key point: 1 H = 1 Wb A⁻¹ = 1 V s A⁻¹.

questions.sub_topic: Magnifying power of a compound microscope
questions.question: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 1 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm, with a tube length of 20 cm. For the final image at infinity (\(D = 25\) cm), its magnifying power is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 100
Given: \(f_o = 1\) cm, \(f_e = 5\) cm, \(L = 20\) cm, \(D = 25\) cm
Formula: \(m \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o} \times \dfrac{D}{f_e}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{L}{f_o} = 20\), \(\dfrac{D}{f_e} = 5\)
Step 2: \(m = 100\)
Common mistake: 120 (D) uses \(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e} = 6\), which applies when the image is at the near point.
Key point: The objective and the eyepiece magnify in turn, so their magnifications multiply.

questions.sub_topic: Power factor of a series LCR circuit
questions.question: In a series LCR circuit, \(R = 40\ \Omega\), \(X_L = 40\ \Omega\) and \(X_C = 10\ \Omega\). The power factor is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.8
Given: \(R = 40\ \Omega\), \(X_L - X_C = 30\ \Omega\)
Formula: \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}\), \(\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z}\)
Step 1: \(Z = \sqrt{1600 + 900} = 50\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(\cos\phi = \dfrac{40}{50} = 0.8\)
Common mistake: 0.6 (A) is \(\dfrac{X_L - X_C}{Z}\), i.e. \(\sin\phi\). 1 (D) assumes resonance.
Key point: Only the resistance takes power, so \(\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z}\).

questions.sub_topic: Uses of four parts of the EM spectrum
questions.question:
Match each radiation in List-I with a use in List-II.

List-I
(A) Microwaves
(B) Infrared
(C) Ultraviolet
(D) X-rays

List-II
(I) Imaging broken bones
(II) Killing germs in water purifiers
(III) Remote controls of TV sets
(IV) Radar for aircraft navigation
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Step 1: Microwaves have short wavelengths suited to radar (IV)
Step 2: Infrared LEDs drive remote controls (III)
Step 3: UV kills bacteria (II)
Step 4: X-rays pass through flesh but not bone (I)
Common mistake: Swapping (C) and (D); both are short-wavelength, but bones are imaged with X-rays.
Key point: Learn each band with one standard use.

questions.sub_topic: Two unequal cells in parallel driving a resistor
questions.question: Cells of emf 6 V and 4 V, each with internal resistance \(1\ \Omega\), are joined in parallel (positive to positive) across a \(2\ \Omega\) resistor. The current in the resistor is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2 A
Given: \(\varepsilon_1 = 6\) V, \(\varepsilon_2 = 4\) V, \(r_1 = r_2 = 1\ \Omega\), \(R = 2\ \Omega\)
Formula: \(\varepsilon_{eq} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_1r_2 + \varepsilon_2r_1}{r_1 + r_2}\), \(r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1 + r_2}\)
Step 1: \(\varepsilon_{eq} = \dfrac{6 + 4}{2} = 5\) V, \(r_{eq} = 0.5\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(I = \dfrac{5}{2 + 0.5} = 2\) A
Common mistake: 4 A (A) adds the emfs as if the cells were in series and ignores internal resistance: \(\dfrac{10}{2.5}\).
Key point: Unequal cells in parallel act like one cell with a weighted-average emf.

questions.sub_topic: Secondary voltage of a step-up transformer
questions.question: An ideal transformer has 200 turns in the primary and 1000 in the secondary. With 220 V a.c. across the primary, the secondary voltage is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1100 V
Given: \(N_p = 200\), \(N_s = 1000\), \(V_p = 220\) V
Formula: \(\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}\)
Step 1: \(V_s = 220 \times 5 = 1100\) V
Common mistake: 44 V (B) inverts the turns ratio.
Key point: More secondary turns step the voltage up and the current down.

questions.sub_topic: Gap between the third bright and fifth dark fringes
questions.question: In Young's double-slit experiment the fringe width is 0.5 mm. The distance between the third bright fringe and the fifth dark fringe on the same side of the central maximum is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.75 mm
Given: \(\beta = 0.5\) mm
Formula: bright fringe \(n\) at \(n\beta\); dark fringe \(n\) at \(\left(n - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\beta\)
Step 1: Third bright: \(3\beta\); fifth dark: \(4.5\beta\)
Step 2: Gap \(= 1.5\beta = 0.75\) mm
Common mistake: 1 mm (B) places the fifth dark fringe at \(5\beta\).
Key point: The first dark fringe is half a fringe width from the centre.

questions.sub_topic: Torque on a dipole at 30° to a uniform field
questions.question: An electric dipole of moment \(4 \times 10^{-9}\) C m makes an angle of \(30^\circ\) with a uniform field of \(5 \times 10^4\) N C⁻¹. The torque on it is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(1 \times 10^{-4}\) N m
Given: \(p = 4 \times 10^{-9}\) C m, \(E = 5 \times 10^4\) N C⁻¹, \(\theta = 30^\circ\)
Formula: \(\tau = pE\sin\theta\)
Step 1: \(pE = 2 \times 10^{-4}\)
Step 2: \(\tau = 2 \times 10^{-4} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 1 \times 10^{-4}\) N m
Common mistake: \(1.73 \times 10^{-4}\) N m (C) uses \(\cos 30^\circ\).
Key point: The torque is greatest at \(90^\circ\) and zero along the field.

questions.sub_topic: Material whose resistivity falls as it is heated
questions.question: Which of these materials shows a decrease in resistivity when its temperature rises?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) silicon
Why: In a semiconductor such as silicon, heating frees more charge carriers across the small band gap, and this outweighs the extra collisions, so resistivity falls (negative temperature coefficient).
Why not the others: Copper's resistivity rises with temperature. Nichrome and manganin are alloys whose resistivity rises only slightly, which is why they are used in heaters and standard resistors.
Key point: Metals: resistivity rises with temperature; semiconductors: it falls.

questions.sub_topic: p–n junction and rectifiers — which claims fail
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Forward bias makes the depletion layer narrower.
(B) In reverse bias a large current flows as soon as the voltage exceeds 0.7 V.
(C) A half-wave rectifier gives output during only one half of each input cycle.
(D) With a 50 Hz input, the output of a full-wave rectifier pulses at 100 Hz.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: in reverse bias only a tiny current (microamperes) flows; 0.7 V is the forward knee voltage of silicon.
Why not the others: (A) the applied voltage opposes the barrier. (C) the diode conducts only when forward biased. (D) both halves give a pulse, so two pulses per cycle. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: A diode conducts easily one way only.

questions.sub_topic: Charge after filling a connected capacitor with a dielectric
questions.question: A \(2\ \mu\text{F}\) air-filled parallel plate capacitor stays connected to a 10 V battery while the gap is completely filled with a dielectric of constant \(K = 5\). The charge on it becomes:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(100\ \mu\text{C}\)
Given: \(C_0 = 2\ \mu\text{F}\), \(K = 5\), \(V = 10\) V (fixed by the battery)
Formula: \(C = KC_0\), \(Q = CV\)
Step 1: \(C = 5 \times 2 = 10\ \mu\text{F}\)
Step 2: \(Q = 10 \times 10 = 100\ \mu\text{C}\)
Common mistake: \(20\ \mu\text{C}\) (A) is the charge before the dielectric. \(4\ \mu\text{C}\) (B) divides by \(K\), as if the battery were removed and \(V\) asked.
Key point: With the battery connected, \(V\) stays fixed and \(Q\) rises \(K\) times.
